archetype.name: Gunslinger (rhythm-dependent)
archetype.definition: A pocket thrower who wins by pushing the ball to the intermediate and deep levels from a clean platform, and who has always paid for that aggression in interceptions.

report.headline: Behind the league's leakiest line, last year's efficiency has become turnovers and sacks.
report.take:
Darnold spent the last two seasons as a QB who could carry an offense: 8.49 yards per attempt, a 5.2 CPOE and 0.162 EPA per play in 2025, after a similar 2024 in Minnesota. The interceptions never left. He ranked 61st of 63 in picks last year and 50th of 60 the year before. Those seasons worked because the efficiency on everything else outran the turnovers. This year it doesn't. He sits at -0.135 EPA per dropback, 36th of 45, with a 4.7% interception rate that ranks 40th. The dossier credits Drew Lock with the Week 2-6 starts, but Darnold took every snap from Week 3 on after playing only 10% of snaps in Week 1 and missing Week 2, so this is effectively his offense.

The main driver is protection. Seattle's offense has the worst hit rate allowed in the league (32nd of 32), and he is pressured on 35.6% of dropbacks, 36th of 37. Under that pressure his own habits aren't the issue. His pressure-to-sack rate (24.1%, 15th) and bad-throw rate (11.4%, 10th) are respectable. The sacks come from how often pressure arrives, not from him holding the ball into it, even with a 3.12-second time to throw. The run game is 30th in EPA, so he lives in third-and-long. His third downs come at an average of 8.1 yards to go and produce -0.543 EPA a play, with a 27.3% conversion rate. That one split explains most of his season.

The numbers also hide that his downfield passing still works. On throws of 10+ air yards he's at +0.283 EPA with a 3.3 CPOE, and his 15 deep attempts have returned +0.693 EPA a throw. The damage is underneath. The screen and behind-the-line game has cost -15.3 EPA on 30 throws, and his targets outside Jaxon Smith-Njigba are mostly negative. AJ Barner sits at -0.515 EPA per target. All seven interceptions came with the game within one score, which is where Seattle's No. 2 defense keeps nearly every game.

The last three weeks look ugly: -0.208 EPA per dropback and an 11.3% sack rate. They also came against three top-10 defenses (LAC 9th, SF 5th, DEN 7th), the last on four days' rest. Against Washington's 26th-ranked unit he threw for 379 and four scores. This is a capable passer stuck behind a bad line and a dead run game. The way out runs through Anthony Bradford returning at guard and Zach Charbonnet stabilizing the ground game, not through Darnold changing who he is.

strengths.title: Downfield accuracy has survived the collapse
strengths.body: Past 10 air yards he's still a positive-EPA passer, and the 15 deep shots have been the best part of his season, with a CPOE of 11.1. That matches the 2024-25 player, who ranked in the top 10 in yards per attempt both years. The deep sample is small and will cool, but the intermediate-plus level is a skill he has shown across seasons.

strengths.title: Red-zone execution has been clean
strengths.body: Inside the 20 he has six touchdowns, no interceptions and a 9.9 CPOE on 17 attempts. That is the only reason his TD rate is league-average despite the rest of the profile. It's an 18-play sample, so expect it to drift down, but it does suggest the turnovers are about reads under duress in the open field, not careless decision-making everywhere.

strengths.title: Handles pressure better than the sacks suggest
strengths.body: His pressure-to-sack rate and bad-throw rate both rank in the top half despite the second-worst pressure rate among qualifiers. His Smith-Njigba connection also still produces at +0.475 EPA per target. When he has a beat to find his top receiver, the offense moves.

concerns.title: Interceptions in one-score games
concerns.body: All seven picks have come with the game within one score, and that game state has cost -35.3 EPA. Interceptions are a career-long trait: 14 last year, 12 the year before. The current 4.7% rate is still above even his own norm, so some regression toward fewer picks is likely. The baseline remains worse than average.

concerns.title: Protection and third-and-long
concerns.body: Seattle allows the league's highest hit rate, and with the run game near the bottom of the league he faces long third downs constantly. His third-down EPA is catastrophic, and his sack rate over the last three weeks has spiked to 11.3%. This is mostly structural rather than a flaw in his game. Bradford's return from IR at guard is the most direct fix.

concerns.title: The quick game is broken
concerns.body: Throws behind the line have lost -15.3 EPA with a 16.7% success rate, so the screens meant to punish pressure aren't working. Barner's -0.515 EPA per target compounds it. With Elijah Arroyo now out for significant time, the tight end group gets thinner, not better.

trend.note: A 379-yard, four-TD game against Washington's weak defense was followed by three straight negative-EPA games against top-10 defenses, with sacks climbing to five in each of the last two. The drop tracks the schedule and the protection as much as his own play.

nextGame.headline: Top-three Chiefs defense, but one that rarely gets home
nextGame.body:
Kansas City's defense ranks 3rd in EPA and 4th against the pass. It is built to choke the short game, allowing -0.261 EPA on short throws, 2nd in the league. Its WR1 coverage has been the stingiest in football by EPA per target, which is a direct problem for an offense that runs through Smith-Njigba. The opening is up top and in the pass rush. The Chiefs are 27th in sack rate and 21st in hit rate, and they're only 14th on deep passes. For a QB whose season has been wrecked by pressure and whose deep ball still works, a defense that doesn't get home is the best matchup trait he could ask for. Tight ends have also scored well above their averages against them.

On Seattle's side, Bradford (a 100%-snap guard when healthy) was designated to return from IR, and Charbonnet has a good chance to play. Either would ease the third-and-long problem. Arroyo is out, leaving Barner to absorb the tight end work the Chiefs tend to give up. Kansas City's own injury list is mostly on offense (two tackles, Rashee Rice), which could slow a top-five Chiefs attack and keep the game in the low-scoring, one-score range Seattle's defense prefers. That is also the game state where Darnold has thrown every interception. Seattle is a 2.5-point favorite with a 42.5 total, and the extra rest after a four-day turnaround helps.

keyMatchups.title: Seattle's line vs. a light rush
keyMatchups.body: Seattle allows the most hits in the league, while Kansas City generates sacks at one of the lowest rates. If that holds, Darnold gets the clean pockets he has rarely had this year. Clean pockets are when his intermediate and deep throws produce.

keyMatchups.title: Short throws into KC's strength
keyMatchups.body: The Chiefs are the second-best defense against short passes, and Darnold's under-10 game is already deeply negative. Dink-and-dunk won't work here. The yardage has to come on intermediate and deep throws, where KC is closer to the middle of the league.

keyMatchups.title: JSN vs. the league's best WR1 defense
keyMatchups.body: Kansas City has allowed the lowest EPA per target to opposing WR1s, and Smith-Njigba carries this passing game. If he's taken away, targets shift to Barner and the WR3 spot, where KC is far more generous. So far Barner hasn't turned targets into value.

nextGame.watch: Whether the pocket stays clean early. If the Chiefs aren't hitting him, look for deep shots to Smith-Njigba and Kupp. If they are, expect another sack-and-turnover game.

restOfSeason.body:
Darnold won't stay at -0.135 EPA per dropback. The accuracy indicators (bad-throw rate, CPOE, deep efficiency) look closer to his 2024-25 self than his results do, and the three-game slump came against three top-10 defenses. Bradford's return and a healthier backfield should cut the third-and-long volume that is driving most of the damage. The interception rate should come down from 4.7%. But picks have been part of his game for years, so a rate near his career norm, around a pick a game, is the realistic target, not a clean sheet.

The ceiling is capped by a run-leaning offense, 27th in pass rate over expected, and a defense good enough to keep games tight and passing volume moderate. I'd expect something like 200-245 yards a game, 1.1-1.6 touchdowns, 0.8-1.2 interceptions and fewer, but still frequent, sacks. That makes him a serviceable starter rather than last year's top-10 producer, unless the protection improves significantly.
swingFactors: Bradford's return and overall pass protection
Whether Charbonnet revives the run game and shortens third downs

confidence.note: Four full games and a jumbled start log, but the protection problem is consistent and his multi-year profile is clear.
